title: Bytecode & Virtual Machines
summary: Most managed runtimes don't execute your source directly — they compile to a portable intermediate instruction format and run that on a virtual machine. See why bytecode exists, and the stack-based vs register-based VM designs that execute it.

slides.markdown:
`javac` doesn't compile Java to x86 instructions. It compiles to **bytecode** — a compact, portable instruction set that no real CPU understands directly, executed instead by a software **virtual machine** (VM).

This is the layer between `the-compilation-pipeline`'s static front-end and `just-in-time-compilation`'s dynamic optimization: bytecode is the *stable target* the compiler emits once, and the VM is the *interpreter* (and later, JIT) that actually runs it.

Two VM designs dominate: **stack-based** (JVM, CLR) and **register-based** (Lua, Dalvik/ART). Same job, different trade-offs — and "what does `javap -c` show you" is one of the most common ways this shows up in interviews.

slides.subTitle: Portability and a stable target
slides.markdown:
Two problems bytecode solves that compiling straight to native machine code doesn't:

- **Portability.** "Write once, run anywhere" only works if "anywhere" means "anywhere a VM for this bytecode exists." The same `.class` file runs on x86, ARM, or a mainframe, because the JVM — not the class file — is what's platform-specific.
- **A stable, simpler compilation target.** Compiler authors emit one well-defined instruction format instead of N native ISAs. The VM's authors, in turn, get one format to optimize deeply (that's what `just-in-time-compilation` does), instead of every language needing its own optimizer per platform.

The cost is an extra layer of indirection: bytecode has to be loaded, verified, and either interpreted or JIT-compiled before it does anything, which is exactly the startup tax `what-a-runtime-provides` described.

The pipeline has a clean handoff point: the compiler's job ends at bytecode, and the VM's job begins there.

slides.subTitle: JVM and CLR bytecode
slides.markdown:
A **stack-based VM** has no named registers. Every instruction pushes to, or pops from, an implicit **operand stack**. To add two numbers, you push both, then run an `add` that pops two and pushes the sum.

The JVM and .NET's CLR both work this way. It makes the instruction set small and simple — most instructions don't need operand fields saying *which* register to use, because the stack is always the source and destination.

The cost: even trivial expressions need several instructions (push, push, add, store) that a register machine could often do in one, and the VM does real work managing that stack on every operation.

slides.subTitle: Lua and Dalvik/ART
slides.markdown:
A **register-based VM** has a set of virtual registers (not real CPU registers — just numbered slots) that instructions read from and write to directly, with operands named in the instruction itself: `add r3, r1, r2` means "add r1 and r2, store in r3."

Lua's VM and Android's Dalvik/ART both use this design. It needs fewer instructions per operation — one `add` instead of push/push/add — at the cost of a wider instruction encoding, since each instruction now carries register operands.

Dalvik specifically chose registers over the JVM's stack model to shrink `.dex` file size and instruction count on memory-constrained mobile devices — a deliberate trade-off for the platform, not a universal "better" design.

For `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`, `javap -c` prints something like:

```
0: iload_1        // push local variable 1 (a) onto the stack
1: iload_2        // push local variable 2 (b) onto the stack
2: iadd           // pop two ints, push their sum
3: ireturn         // pop and return the top of the stack
```

Read it stack-first: `iload_1` and `iload_2` each push one operand, `iadd` consumes both and leaves one result, `ireturn` hands that result back to the caller. Four bytecode instructions for one `+` — this is the instruction-count cost of the stack model, and it's exactly the kind of trivial, repetitive sequence a JIT compiler collapses into a single native `add` instruction once the method gets hot.

slides.sectionTitle: Stack-based vs register-based, head to head
slides.markdown:
| | Stack-based (JVM, CLR) | Register-based (Lua, Dalvik) |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction count per op | Higher (multiple push/pop steps) | Lower (operands named directly) |
| Instruction encoding size | Smaller (no register operands) | Larger (carries register numbers) |
| Compiler simplicity | Simpler code generation | Needs register allocation at compile time |
| Typical use case | General-purpose managed runtimes | Embedded/mobile, size-constrained targets |

Neither is strictly faster — a JIT erases most of the difference once bytecode is compiled to native code, since the JIT's own internal representation isn't stack- or register-bound. The choice mostly affects **interpreted** performance and `.class`/`.dex` file size, which is exactly why Android picked registers for a memory-constrained device and the JVM (designed in the 1990s for a different constraint set) picked a stack.

Before any JIT kicks in, both VM styles run the same basic shape of loop: fetch the next bytecode instruction, dispatch on its opcode (usually a big switch statement or a jump table), execute it, repeat.

This is genuinely simple — and genuinely slow relative to native code, because every single bytecode instruction pays dispatch overhead that a compiled native instruction doesn't. That overhead is the entire reason `just-in-time-compilation` exists: it's cheaper to spend time compiling a hot method to native code once than to keep paying dispatch overhead on every iteration of a hot loop, forever.

A common mistake: hearing "the JVM interprets bytecode" and concluding Java is permanently interpreter-slow, the way a naive script interpreter is.

That's true only for the first, cold execution of a method. HotSpot (the JVM's execution engine) starts every method interpreted, but promotes hot ones to compiled native code within milliseconds to seconds of real use (`just-in-time-compilation`, `the-jvm-deep-dive`). Steady-state JVM throughput on a hot loop is routinely within a small factor of C — nowhere near "interpreted language" slow.

The honest framing: bytecode + a VM is a *starting point* for execution, and whether it stays interpreter-slow or reaches native speed depends entirely on whether the runtime has a JIT. CPython, notably, mostly doesn't (`dynamic-language-runtimes-v8-and-cpython`), which is why the "interpreted = slow" stereotype sticks to it more fairly than to the JVM.

Because a `.class` file can come from anywhere — the network, a third-party JAR, a plugin — the JVM **verifies** bytecode before running it: checking that stack operations are balanced, types match at every operation, jumps land on valid instruction boundaries, and access modifiers (private/public) aren't violated.

This is a real safety boundary, not a formality — it's what lets the JVM sandbox untrusted code (historically, applets) and refuse to run bytecode a hand-crafted or corrupted `.class` file might contain. Verification is also why a JVM rejects some technically-runnable bytecode a hostile tool could construct: safety is enforced structurally, not just by trusting the compiler that produced it.

Bytecode and a VM interpreter loop is the baseline every runtime in this group builds on:

- **`just-in-time-compilation`** — how the VM stops interpreting hot bytecode and compiles it to native code instead.
- **`the-jvm-deep-dive`** — HotSpot's concrete class loading, memory areas, and JIT tiers built on top of this stack model.
- **`the-clr-and-dotnet-runtime`** — the CLR's IL, which is stack-based like the JVM's, with a different JIT strategy.
- **`dynamic-language-runtimes-v8-and-cpython`** — what changes when the source language is dynamically typed rather than statically typed like Java or C#.
